entries.meaning: Elephants roar, bells thunder, horses neigh, chariots rumble, and drums challenge the clouds so loudly that no ear can distinguish its own side from another. A vast crowd fills the king’s gate and dust rises to the palace battlements, while women watch from terraces with auspicious lamps. Sumantra prepares two superb chariots with horses that shame the sun’s steeds: one for Vasiṣṭha and the royal company, the other a radiant vehicle for Daśaratha, who mounts after remembering Śiva, his guru, Gaurī and Gaṇeśa.

words.grammar: locative plural witness form in the palace-fortification image

entries.meaning: Daśaratha beside Vasiṣṭha shines like Indra beside the gods’ preceptor. After completing family and Vedic rites and inspecting every preparation, the king remembers Rāma, receives his guru’s leave, and sets out to the sound of the conch. Gods shower flowers; heavenly and earthly musicians fill sky and city with auspicious song, shehnais, bells, jokes and skilled performances. Princes dance their horses to drumbeats so expertly that professional actors stare, lose the rhythm, and miss their steps.

words.grammar: plural activity noun governed by करहिं in the foot-soldiers' display

entries.meaning: The incomparable procession advances amid a full array of favourable omens: a bird takes food on the left; a crow calls auspiciously on the right; a mongoose is seen; a threefold breeze blows gently; married women approach with full vessels and children; a small bird repeatedly appears; a cow nurses her calf face-on; a line of deer turns to the right; omen-birds promise welfare; and two learned Brahmins meet them bearing books, together with curds and fish. It is as if every omen gathered at once to ensure that all desires would come true.

words.grammar: regional bird-name in an omen catalogue

entries.meaning: All omens come easily to Daśaratha, whose son is the beautiful embodied Brahman; the groom is Rāma, the bride Sītā, and the fathers are the holy Daśaratha and Janaka. The wedding party proceeds with elephants, horses and resounding drums. Knowing Raghu’s banner is coming, Janaka has bridges built across rivers and magnificent lodgings placed along the route, supplied like heaven with food, beds and clothing to each guest’s taste. At news of their approach, a splendid escort sets out on elephants, chariots, horses and foot.

Janaka sends the welcoming party with golden pitchers and trays, graceful vessels full of nectar-like dishes, fruit, excellent gifts, ornaments, garments, great jewels, birds, deer, horses, elephants, curds, flattened rice and innumerable auspicious offerings. When the hosts see the procession their bodies thrill; the wedding party sees the magnificent reception and sounds its drums in joy. Both sides hurry forward to meet, like two oceans of bliss abandoning their shores and flowing together.

words.grammar: adverb describing the two parties advancing together to meet

entries.meaning: Gods shower flowers, heavenly women sing, and drums sound while the welcoming gifts are respectfully placed before Daśaratha. He accepts them lovingly and distributes them as rewards to petitioners. After worship and honour, the hosts lead the guests over rich cloths to a beautiful, fully provisioned lodging. Sītā, knowing the party has arrived, quietly reveals a measure of her divine power: she summons all mystic perfections and sends them to provide hospitality, carrying the complete wealth and pleasures of heaven.

Each guest finds every heavenly comfort readily available in his lodging, yet no one perceives the secret of the abundance and all praise Janaka. Raghunātha alone recognizes Sītā’s greatness and rejoices at its loving purpose. When Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa hear that their father has arrived, boundless joy rises within, but modesty keeps them from asking their guru for leave despite their longing. Viśvāmitra understands, embraces both brothers with tears of joy, and leads them toward Daśaratha like a lake approaching the thirsty.

Daśaratha repeatedly prostrates to Viśvāmitra and places the dust of his feet upon his head; Kauśika embraces him, blesses him and asks after his welfare. When Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa bow, the king’s delight cannot be contained: he clasps them to his heart and unbearable separation vanishes like life returning to a corpse. They bow to Vasiṣṭha and the Brahmins, then lovingly embrace Bharata and Śatrughna. The gracious brothers greet townspeople, relatives, caste-fellows, petitioners, ministers and friends with the honour proper to each.

Seeing Rāma cools the whole wedding party, and its love cannot be described. Daśaratha’s four sons beside him look like the four human aims embodied. Janakpur’s people rejoice, gods shower flowers and celestial performers dance; Śatānanda, Brahmins, ministers, bards and heralds honour the king and his party before the reception group takes leave. Because the procession arrived before the wedding hour, the city’s joy grows still more, and people beg Brahmā to lengthen day and night so they may behold the matchless pair and the two peerless kings.

The townspeople say Vaidehī is the embodied fruit of Janaka’s merit and Rāma the embodied fruit of Daśaratha’s; no one has worshipped Śiva like these fathers or gained an equal reward. They count themselves a treasury of merit merely for being born in Janakpur and seeing Jānakī and Rāma. They look forward to watching the wedding and imagine Janaka repeatedly inviting Sītā home, so that the two brothers—lovely as millions of Loves—will return and become honoured guests of their eyes.
